title: Continuous Measurement of Quantum Axion Dark Matter
authors: Yunjia Bao, Dhong Yeon Cheong, Nicholas L. Rodd, Joey Takach, Lian-Tao Wang, Kevin Zhou
abstract: We provide a fully quantum-mechanical description of the continuous measurement of wavelike dark matter. Our focus is cavity haloscopes, although our results inform a broad range of axion searches. We extend the input-output formalism by treating the axion as a quantum field, finding how its quantum state is imprinted onto higher-order moments of observables of the outgoing transmission-line modes. We further develop a novel measurement-record formalism, which computes the joint probability distribution of all measurement outcomes and is well suited to studying the axion in the time domain. With it, we compute the exact axion-induced number distribution for the first time, demonstrating that it is not Poisson. We argue that virialized axion dark matter is expected to be in a Gaussian quantum state, and show that number or quadrature measurements can distinguish this from the predictions of a coherent state or even a Bose-Einstein condensate. Finally, we show that intrinsically quantum effects, such as those from Fock or squeezed axion states, are far too weak to detect.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous, fully quantum-mechanical framework for analyzing the continuous measurement of axion dark matter in cavity haloscopes. By introducing a novel measurement-record formalism, the authors compute exact quantum statistics, demonstrating that the expected dark matter state is non-Poissonian and distinct from classical or simple quantum predictions.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a fully quantum-mechanical description of the continuous measurement process for wavelike axion dark matter.
main_result: The axion-induced number distribution is shown to be non-Poissonian, and quantum measurements can distinguish the expected virialized Gaussian state from coherent or Bose-Einstein condensate predictions.
method: The authors develop and utilize a novel measurement-record formalism (Schrödinger picture) alongside the standard input-output formalism (Heisenberg picture) to track the joint probability distribution of measurement outcomes.
model_or_system: The system involves axion dark matter interacting with a microwave cavity haloscope. The analysis treats the axion as a quantum field, coupling to the cavity's transmission-line modes.
key_observables: Number distribution, quadrature measurements, and the joint probability distribution of all measurement outcomes (the measurement record).
important_parameters: Axion coupling strengths, cavity quality factor, and the characteristic timescale for DM evolution ($	au_{DM}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the virialized axion dark matter is in a Gaussian quantum state, and the measurement-record formalism is employed to overcome limitations of moment-based approaches.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the continuous monitoring process, comparing the input-output formalism to the measurement-record formalism, and showing that a coherent state yields Poisson statistics while a Gaussian state deviates significantly.
paper_structure: The paper builds the quantum description using the input-output formalism, introduces the novel measurement-record formalism for time-domain analysis, and applies this framework to compute exact number and quadrature statistics for axion-induced signals.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it applies advanced quantum measurement theory (measurement-record formalism) to a concrete problem in quantum optics and particle astrophysics (axion detection), providing rigorous diagnostics for quantum state characterization.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of this work. (a) The axion-induced signal in a haloscope is continuously monitored at the end of a transmission line by a photon counting or quadrature measurement. Our formalism can track an arbitrary axion quantum state through the detection pipeline to its impact on either observable. (b) The setup can be equivalently described using the standard input-output formalism or the measurement record formalism. The former involves operators in Heisenberg picture, naturally yielding moments and correlators, whilst the latter tracks states in Schr¨odinger picture, yielding the joint probability distribution of the measurement record. Figure 2. A schematic of the logic underpinning the input-output formalism: a single cavity mode c is coupled to the axion, measurement, and loss ports. The axion port provides the signal that drives the cavity, the measurement port carries the output signal that continuously monitors the cavity, and the loss port models additional dissipation in the cavity. In input-output theory, each is viewed as a transmission line into the cavity. Our depiction here is inspired by Ref. [58].

Figure 3. Toy model of a string (transmission line) coupled to a classical harmonic oscillator (cavity mode): the input field of an incoming waveform interacts with the oscillator, before producing an outgoing waveform that heads back down the line to be detected. Once the system is quantized, the line can be described by a series of discrete modes b as defined in Eq. (3.14).

Figure 4. Schematic comparison of the expectation values of the quadrature PSD (blue) and the differential photon-number spectrum (orange) assuming the cavity is driven solely by the axion field, with no thermal noise. Though the PSD S[ω] is two-sided and has a noise floor due to vacuum fluctuations, its expectation value carries the same information as ⟨Nout[ω]⟩. Yet as we discuss in Sec. 3.4, the fluctuations of these observables can differ significantly.

Figure 5. The impact on the cavity P-function if we projectively measure number (left) or quadrature (right) at the end of the transmission line, for a cavity initially in a thermal Gaussian state, and definite values for the number and quadrature outcomes. To emphasize the difference with respect to projective measurements of the cavity itself, we take θ = π/8, where the effect is strong, though in practice θ ≪1 and the posterior cavity state remains far closer to its initial form.
